passage:
The colony's Independence Day drawing prize went to Nilesh, for his kite-filled sky. Anand's own painting, the one he'd worked on for three evenings, didn't even get a mention. His stomach dropped. Everyone turned to look at him, because he and Nilesh were always together.

Anand made himself clap. Then he walked over and thumped Nilesh on the shoulder. "Well done, yaar. The orange kites are the best bit." Nilesh beamed.

At home, Anand sat on the kitchen stool while Mumma rolled dough. "I'm happy for him. But I really wanted it. Is that bad?"

Mumma dusted flour off her hands. "It's not bad. You felt jealous and still clapped. That's hard. Now tell me about your painting."

qa.q: What did Nilesh's winning drawing show?
qa.a: A kite-filled sky.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling as he clapped for Nilesh?
qa.a: Disappointed and a bit jealous, since his three evenings of work got no mention, yet he chose to celebrate his friend anyway.

qa.q: Why was talking to Mumma at home healthier than pretending?
qa.a: Naming the jealousy in private let Anand feel it without hiding it, and Mumma showed that feeling it and still clapping is a real skill.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Anand congratulates him?
qa.a: Delighted and proud, especially since his best friend praises a specific part, the orange kites.

grounding: It shows a child congratulating a friend on a prize while disappointed, and naming his envy privately to a parent rather than pretending it isn't there.

passage:
Saturday: At Dadi's house in Jaipur, Vijay bent and touched her feet the moment he came in. Dadi pressed his head. "Jeete raho." He felt the old warm feeling from every summer he'd spent there.

Monday: Back home in Pune, Devika Aunty from the flat below was locking her door. Vijay pressed his palms together. "Namaste, Devika Aunty-ji." She laughed. "Aunty is enough, beta. But thank you." He grinned; in this building, "Aunty" already meant respect.

Thursday: At his friend Imtiaz's house, Imtiaz's grandfather sat by the window. Vijay started to bend, then saw Imtiaz touch his hand to his forehead. "Adaab, Dadajaan." Vijay copied him carefully. The old man smiled and waved them in.

qa.q: What did Dadi say when Vijay touched her feet?
qa.a: "Jeete raho."

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he touched Dadi's feet on Saturday?
qa.a: Warm and nostalgic, feeling the old comfort of every summer spent at Dadi's house.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that was wise on Thursday?
qa.a: He paused and watched Imtiaz, then copied the adaab greeting, fitting his respect to that family's custom.

qa.q: How did Devika Aunty react to "Aunty-ji"?
qa.a: She was amused and touched, laughing that "Aunty" is enough while thanking him for the respect.

grounding: It shows a child showing respect to elders by touching feet, a namaste with a respectful address and an adaab, with the form varying by family and faith.

passage:
I'm Afreen, and last year I learned that the same words can feel different. When Rajni drew the banyan tree for our class wall, I told her, "The roots look like they're really moving." She went pink and said thank you, and the next week she helped me with my shading without being asked.

Then there was Sohail. Every morning he told somebody their handwriting was "amazing", and every afternoon he asked that same person to lend him their notebook. After a while nobody smiled at his compliments; they just held their notebooks tighter.

When Rajni thanked me for helping her study for the Hindi test, I realised that real compliments and thank-yous go both ways.

qa.q: What did Rajni draw for the class wall?
qa.a: The banyan tree.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when Afreen praised the moving roots?
qa.a: Pleased and a little shy, as she went pink 😊, and grateful enough to help with the shading the next week.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's compliment land better than Sohail's?
qa.a: It was sincere and specific, about the roots, and came with no request, while Sohail's praise always came before asking for a notebook.

qa.q: How did classmates come to see Sohail's compliments?
qa.a: As a way to get favours, so they stopped smiling and held their notebooks tighter.

grounding: It is a child's reflection on sincere, specific compliments and thanks that go both ways, compared with compliments used to gain favours.

passage:
The rain came down in sheets, the school bus had already gone, and Imran's cycle wasn't in the stand. Only a cut lock lay in the mud. Imran just stood there, water dripping off his nose.

Divyansh felt his own stomach drop, the way it had when his cricket bat vanished from the park last year. Poor Imran, he thought, and then: No, not poor Imran. I know this feeling.

He wanted to throw an arm round Imran and talk about the bat. But maybe Imran didn't want that. "Do you want company, or a minute alone?"

Imran wiped his face. "A minute. Then walk home with me?"

Divyansh stepped back under the shed roof and waited. Then they went to tell the guard together.

qa.q: What lay in the mud where the cycle had been?
qa.a: A cut lock.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he saw the empty stand?
qa.a: His stomach dropped along with Imran's: he felt the loss with him, remembering his own vanished bat, not just sorry for him.

qa.q: Why was asking "Do you want company?" wiser than an arm round the shoulders?
qa.a: Divyansh's guess might have been wrong; asking let Imran choose a minute alone first, then company.

qa.q: What was Imran likely feeling as he stood dripping in the rain?
qa.a: Shocked and upset at losing his cycle, and needing a moment before he could talk.

grounding: It shows a child feeling with a friend and not just sorry for him, and asking whether he wants company instead of assuming.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage:
Sunday

Samir's first swimming race today. By the pool his hands were shaking and he kept saying he felt sick. I said, "You can do it! Don't be scared!" He snapped, "I AM scared, okay?" Oops.

So I tried again. "Okay, you're nervous. That's normal. Remember what Coach says: count your strokes to the wall, like in practice. Just the counting." He nodded and started muttering "one, two, three" under his breath.

He came third! Afterwards he said the counting was the only thing in his head, and that it helped more than "you can do it". I'm going to remember that for my own exams.

Dhruv

qa.q: What place did Samir come in the race?
qa.a: Third.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when Samir snapped, "I AM scared, okay?"
qa.a: A bit embarrassed and sorry ("Oops"), realising that "Don't be scared" had brushed aside Samir's real, nervous feelings.

qa.q: What made Dhruv's second try more helpful?
qa.a: Dhruv accepted the nerves as normal and gave a concrete step: count the strokes to the wall, like in practice 👍

qa.q: How did Samir see the two kinds of encouragement afterwards?
qa.a: Samir said the counting helped more than "you can do it", because it gave his mind one thing to hold on to.

grounding: It is a child's diary about encouraging a nervous friend before a race, learning that acknowledging the nerves and giving a concrete step helps most.

passage:
Tuesday

I have to write this because I feel bad. In art I bumped Vinita's clay elephant off the shelf, and its trunk snapped. First I said, "Sorry if you're upset," and walked off, which was rubbish. Vinita didn't talk to me all through lunch. At home, Mum asked what I was actually sorry for.

Today before the bell, I went up to Vinita and said, "I knocked your elephant off and broke the trunk. I'm sorry. Can I stay after school and help you fix it, or make a new trunk with you?" Vinita looked at me for a long time, then said, "You do the glue. I'll do the shape." It looks a bit wonky now, but she smiled.

Elizabeth

qa.q: What part of Vinita's clay elephant snapped?
qa.a: Its trunk.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after the first "Sorry if you're upset"?
qa.a: Guilty and uncomfortable, calling it rubbish, especially when Vinita stayed silent all through lunch.

qa.q: What made the second apology better?
qa.a: Elizabeth named the specific act, "I knocked your elephant off and broke the trunk", said sorry and offered to help fix it.

qa.q: How did Vinita likely feel about the two apologies?
qa.a: The vague one probably felt careless and left her hurt; the specific one with an offer of help made her willing to fix it together and smile.

grounding: It is a child's diary contrasting a vague sorry with an apology that names the act and offers to help repair it.

passage:
I'm Trisha. When I was nine, Irfan tore the cover off my favourite comic because I wouldn't lend it to him. The next day he said sorry, and I said, "It's okay, let's play," really fast. The truth is, it wasn't okay. I just hated fighting. We played carrom and I pretended to forget.

Two weeks later he grabbed my new pencil box and threw it when I said no. This time I didn't say "It's okay." I said, "I'll forgive you, and I still want to be friends. But if you grab my things again, I won't lend you anything."

He went quiet. He never grabbed again. I think that was the first time I forgave someone properly.

qa.q: What did Irfan tear?
qa.a: The cover off Trisha's favourite comic.

qa.q: Why did Trisha say "It's okay, let's play" so fast the first time?
qa.a: Trisha hated fighting and felt uneasy about conflict, so said it to smooth things over while still feeling hurt.

qa.q: What was different about Trisha's second forgiveness?
qa.a: Trisha forgave and kept the friendship, but set a clear limit: grabbing again would mean no more lending.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when Trisha set that limit?
qa.a: Irfan went quiet, probably surprised and a little ashamed to see the grabbing would not simply be brushed aside.

grounding: It is a child's look back at a quick forgiveness given to avoid conflict, and a later forgiveness that kept the friendship but refused to accept the behaviour again.

passage:
Exams started on Monday, and the clinic was two bus rides away in town, a trip that meant Amma losing a day's wages. So when her tummy hurt on Thursday, Kalyani said nothing. On Friday she said, "It's nothing."

But Ira didi noticed she'd left her rice, and that she kept pressing her right side when she thought no one was looking. Didi sat down beside her. "Show me where. Is it sharp, or dull, or cramping? If five is the worst ever, how bad?"

Kalyani pointed low on her right side. "Sharp. Four. Since yesterday."

Didi's face went serious. "Thank you for telling me properly. That's not a keep-quiet pain. I'm getting Amma, and we're going to the clinic today."

qa.q: Where did Kalyani point to?
qa.a: Low on her right side.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani keep saying "It's nothing"?
qa.a: She was worried about causing a fuss: the clinic was far, Amma would lose a day's wages and exams were coming, so she played the pain down.

qa.q: How did Ira didi help Kalyani describe the pain?
qa.a: She asked where it was, what kind it was and how bad on a scale of five, so Kalyani could say, "Sharp. Four. Since yesterday."

qa.q: What made Ira didi notice something was wrong?
qa.a: The change in behaviour: Kalyani left her rice and kept pressing her side when she thought no one was looking.

grounding: It shows a child playing down pain to avoid fuss, and an older sister noticing changed behaviour, helping her describe place, kind and level, and acting that day.

passage:
At Farhan Bhai's bag shop, Madhav held up the blue bag with the rocket on it. "I like this one better. Please?"

Farhan Bhai named the price. Mummy winced; it was almost double the plain grey one, and the electricity bill was due. "Madhav, I can't do this one this month."

"But the grey one looks like an old man's bag! And the rocket one has a bottle pocket. Mine always leaks on my books."

Mummy thought. "The pocket is a fair reason. Farhan Bhai, does any cheaper bag have a bottle pocket?"

Farhan Bhai pulled down a green one with a side pocket. No rocket. Madhav frowned, then grinned. "Can I draw a rocket on it myself?"
"Deal."

qa.q: What did the green bag have?
qa.a: A side pocket.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when Mummy said she couldn't buy the rocket bag this month?
qa.a: Disappointed and a bit frustrated, which is why he pushed back with reasons like the leaking bottle.

qa.q: How did Mummy keep Madhav's trust while saying no?
qa.a: She explained the limit honestly, took his bottle-pocket reason seriously and found a cheaper bag that met that need.

qa.q: How might Farhan Bhai see the negotiation?
qa.a: Farhan Bhai likely sees a family watching its spending and helps by bringing out a cheaper bag with a pocket instead of pushing the dearer one.

grounding: It shows a child stating a preference and giving reasons, and a parent explaining a limit respectfully while meeting the real need.

passage:
I'm Jaya, Manoj's twin sister, and I watched the whole Sunday match from the wall. When the teams were picked, Manoj said, "That's not fair. All the Class 7 boys are on one side." He was right, and Coach Bhatia swapped two players. Everybody agreed.

But then Manoj kept going. "Coach, Kunal's foot was over the line!" "Coach, Deepu took two extra balls!" "Coach, they're whispering!" By the tenth time, even his own team groaned.

Coach called him over. "You've got a good eye for fairness, Manoj. Tell me the big things. The small ones, sort out with the player, politely." I don't know if Manoj was embarrassed, but he didn't shout "Coach" again that day.

qa.q: Who swapped two players?
qa.a: Coach Bhatia.

qa.q: What might Manoj have been feeling when he kept calling "Coach"?
qa.a: Probably a strong, genuine sense that things should be fair, and some frustration; Jaya can't tell whether he felt embarrassed afterwards.

qa.q: What guidance did Coach Bhatia give on tone?
qa.a: Report the big things to the coach and sort out the small ones politely with the player, rather than telling on every little thing.

qa.q: How did Manoj's own team react by the tenth complaint?
qa.a: They got fed up and groaned, seeing it as tale-telling rather than fairness.

grounding: It is a sister's account of a child's genuine fairness complaint being upheld, then sliding into tale-telling until a coach guides his tone.
